title: SORA, AI and the end of commercial cinema

commenti.body:
Every decade since the beginning of human reckoning, humans have expressed fear that new technology will inhibit the human ability or desire for expression, and yet every single time, all that happened was that humanity gained another way to express.

The transitional times will be violent, and we’ll have to get used to digital art being something that can be mass-produced. But as a whole, I welcome a turn away from mass-produced and commercial cinema. Consider how every single generation’s technology fear was looking ahead, while always assuming the ‘present’ state to be the ideal one, the one where technology has advanced just enough to be good without being harmful. It’s always an illusion.

As for cinema being something that, in the future, will be a means to make a living for *fewer* people - that has always been the cost of technology, and even without AI we’re entering a century in which the idea of work-to-make-a-living becomes increasingly unstable and unviable. This is neither the fault of generative art, nor is it the main driver.

If the audience wants this new form of media expression it will happen. Maybe there will be a honeymoon period and there will be a return to hand-crafted media some decades down the line. Maybe not. Either way this is happening, as it has always happened.

I mean as much as I want to remain hopeful considering that I wish to go into film myself, you have to admit that there is a *vast* difference between new technologies such as cameras or cgi and AI. AI is not really a new art form, it's the old art forms except that you are basically just telling someone else to do the hard work for you.

At the end of the day, there will come a time when there will be no noticable difference between meticulously "prompt-engineering" a film and simply typing "generate a masterpiece for me". Part of the appeal of filmmaking is being able to show other people "hey, look at what we made", but when literally anyone can generate an amazing film by just typing in a sentence I really don't think anyone will give a shit. There's something incredibly absurd (in a bad way) about making a film that nobody will watch.

I’m not sure the fear is misplaced, but the subject certainly is. 

AI is a hype bubble right now. The hyperbolic claims coming out of Silicon Valley should be plainly seen for what they are: the newest vehicle for magical thinking that will drive VC investment and IPOs. And an excuse for executives to gut their companies, save millions in the short term, and collect enormous bonuses. 

It’s not that there is no merit to what we are now calling AI. But the actual creative and economic impact, once the crash happens and things normalize, is going to be something more akin to the cell phone and less to… whatever the fuck they’re trying to convince us it is now. It’s a useful tool. It might very well replace some niches of job in some industries, or if not replace then reduce the number of positions overall. 

What is actually gutting cinema is hyper-capitalism. Working conditions are deteriorating, the quality of the biggest films is tanking, and streaming services are disrupting traditional distribution networks. It’s far from dead, and I don’t think it’s doomed, but there’s a lot of bad going on right now. Patrick Willems has a great video discussing the causes. It’s not any one thing, it’s a lot of things, most of which are connected to economics and shitty incentives. 

AI is just another part of that. Don’t buy into the hype. It’s a thing, it will be disruptive, but it’s not going to be a “forget everything you think you know about cinema”
This. Been shooting in snow and carrying heavy equipment and prepping and saving, and now this shit hits.
I hope so. Really just have to carry on with the current project and we'll see what's up soon enough.

Other than your hopes and hunches, anything tangible to show that AI is in a hype bubble and is going to crash? Because this just sounds like personal bias, especially after seeing the Sora development yesterday. In one year we progressed from the Will Smith eating pasta video into something that has legitimate commercial viability- and that's just what their showing the public.

You have to realize that that is the difference between what is available to the public (Will Smith eating) and Sora is what PEAK results of billions of dollars of resource has brought them. You can clearly see it's cherrypicked footage. It will be a long time before it is financially viable for the public to have access to this technology, if it even does. This was an exercise in research to get them a clearer view of the goals needed for AGI.

Let us not forget that the world and humanity has faced hard limitations towards innovation. That exponential progress towards machine learning could go either way but it is far from safe from the patterns of human innovation. Lots of things have plateaud despite offering a lot of promise. May it be economical viability or physical limitations, nothing is exempt. From energy to travel and many other things.

Moore's Law has held true for over 50 years now. Highly doubt we'll be hitting the AI plateau anytime soon, the technology is cutting edge yet also in an infantile stage of development. Even if processing power maxes out, there is a ton of room of optimization and efficiency to increase overall output.

Moore's Law is non applicable in the traditional sense anymore. It is nearly hitting its physical limitation. And the potential for it swings both ways. Again. Consider that they have been working on this not as a product, but as a research exercise for AGI for a long time that we didn't know about. It took them so much energy. So many specialized GPUs to get here. And here it is, presented as novelty. Throwing compute and throwing more data isn't the only they're doing and as they get further it starts to cost more. As long as we have technological diminishing returns it will always haunt the potential of machine learning.
I work in data science and what I've seen doesn't fit this assertion. Think the developments over next five years will give you pause and reevaluation.

Yeah and Bill Gates worked in tech and said the internet was a fad and will burn out eventually. I'm quite flippant on my attitude on this but don't get it twisted. Everything is subject to the laws of nature and you can consider the way and pace we innovate at is part of it. Data is accurate until it eventually isn't. I think you'd know that more than anybody else. I'd just concede your guess is more educated than mine, if I were to believe you. Which is fine. Discussion is good.

I mean, you're correct that capitalism continues to make living an earning (for some) hard, and that this is the largest effect on working conditions at this point in time.

However, I really think you're underestimating the impact of AI in the short to medium term. AI (in its current incarnation) is still in its infancy and it's clearly capable already of feats that endanger entire avenues of making money from art.

Stock footage will soon be gone (and why not?), and commercial art may do the same. Art-art, provoking emotional response and thought, is not immune; in the fullness of time, buying human-made art will be a statement, not the only option.

I work in healthcare, so when I think of data science I'm thinking about cancer survival rates, not AI generated art. This is just a heads up that your flippant attitude towards the technology will eventually bite you in the ass if it doesn't kill us all first.

It will bite me in the ass how? I think you're confused. You want to accost me for not addressing the possibility that every innovation that takes off can eventually be miniscule or pedestrian in our ever changing lives? It can happen. We've seen a lot as the human race. I only claim one thing to be predictable, is that the world will always be unpredictable. Now if you want machine learning to succeed then its important that you keep a clear head for everything that can happen and recognize that even where it is now is potentially beneficial to your line of work. 

Let's just hope it actually helps your industry more instead of rotting society from within. Until then I am able to concede that this is a great unknown.

I'd say we are safe for now... The scary part is if legislation or lack of lets this steam roll not only our industry but most.  Misinformation at it's peak shoveled down our throats from all angles.  Will content need to be made aware that is AI or partially AI created?  I can see a world where corporations invest in their own AI technologies that will be an internal self-learning cycle to efficiently create high end content.  Hell, even that is probably already in the works with some companies.    
What I'm more interested to see develop is the awareness of consumers and how it affects them.  After the shock and awe of it "looks so close to real life!", we will adapt and become better at picking things out and noticing what has been altered.  Will we care?
You sounded reasonable at first, but now you're engaging in hyperbole. It sounds like you're nervous. I am too. But the fact is, we don't yet know how AI will disrupt industries.
I'm not nervous, I'm excited to see the disruption. That disruption is societal progress IMO. If it doesn't kill us all it will empower us more than any other technical advancement.

I'm glad you're excited. I think, even with amazing things happening, it's going to be mostly a very rough time for most people. The level of anxiety about our existing jobs, a potential market collapse, the further erosion of truth, an even faster growing wealth divide. For many, the loss of a sense of purpose/a meaningful way to contribute to society.

Those are fair points but the only one listed I'm genuinely concerned about is the erosion of truth. All of my AI concerns have to do with the narcissistic & self-serving individuals that might be behind the tool than the tool itself. Individuals using AI for their own gain at the expense of others will a very ugly part of this new reality we're going to have to get used to. 

In terms of jobs and the economy, I have little concern because they aren't zero-sum in nature. The job market is a reflection of our society. Many existing jobs will be eliminated, others will be created in response. For many, AI will empower individuals in a more fulfilling way to contribute to society and their own personal goals. It'll be easier than ever to create your own film, write your own novel, build your own small business, etc. using AI tools compared to those currently existing. The end result will have to stand on its own merits, but the work will be completed differently.

I think you are missing some warning signs about the economy. If 30% of people lost their jobs in the next 5 years it would be a catastrophe that would shake our economics and politics to their cores. But a lot more jobs could be lost before new ones are gained.

As far as it being easier to make novels and films, that simply means the market will be absolutely overwhelmed with content. And it will be very difficult to make consistent good money from creative pursuits, maybe impossible for most.

Yes, I have no confidence that first point will occur. It's pure fear mongering and speculation, IMO. 

That second point is just cynicism. Quality will rise to the top and curation will be valued more than ever.
What you say is equally as speculative.
